t: Introduction: the concept of a firearm injury
n: In this lecture we study firearm injuries. A firearm injury is an injury inflicted by the injuring factor, that is, a projectile set in motion from a weapon by the energy of powder gases. Injuries from the explosion of an artillery shell, mine or grenade, and from various explosive substances, are also counted as firearm injuries. In practice such injuries are less common than injuries from blunt and sharp objects, but law enforcement bodies investigate them thoroughly.

We consider the distinctive features of firearm injuries. Unlike blunt and sharp objects, firearm injuries are related to the design characteristics of weapons and ammunition. The injuring projectile has a relatively small mass but moves at a very high speed. The injury may be inflicted even from a great distance. Attention: besides the mechanical factor, thermal, chemical and other kinds of action also occur. Therefore it is not enough to look for mechanical damage alone.

We consider the two groups in forensic medicine. Injuries are conventionally divided into two groups: firearm injuries and blast trauma. Firearm injuries are damage inflicted by weapons and are important in peacetime as well. Blast trauma is damage in cases of explosion. Injuries from the explosion of a shell, mine or grenade are observed mainly in combat conditions. In peacetime, cases involving firearms and explosions are significant for examination.

We study the classification of firearms. By purpose, weapons are divided into military, hunting, sporting, gas and special types. A weapon made at a special factory is called typical, and a home-made or modified one atypical. Military weapons are divided into artillery and small arms. Small arms may be individual, for example a rifle and a pistol, or crew-served, for example a machine gun. That is, the type of weapon is determined by its purpose and method of manufacture.

We speak about the barrel and calibre. The barrel is a metal tube; the high pressure in it drives the projectile towards the target. The grooves impart rotation to the bullet, so the bullet's velocity, range and accuracy increase. A military barrel has 4-6 grooves. By calibre, small calibre is up to 6 mm, medium calibre 7-9 mm, and large calibre 10 mm and above. In hunting weapons the calibre is 10-32, most often 12 and 16. In a smooth-bore hunting weapon, the larger the calibre number, the smaller the diameter of the bore.

Quick questions: types of weapon. First question: to which type does a home-made rifle, or one with a shortened barrel, belong? Answer: atypical weapon. Second question: which weapons are short-barrelled? Answer: the pistol and the revolver; long-barrelled weapons are the rifle and the carbine. Third question: what do the grooves in the barrel give? Answer: rotation of the bullet, as a result of which velocity and accuracy increase. Attention, there is a risk of error: in a smooth barrel a large calibre number does not mean a large diameter; on the contrary, the diameter decreases.

We consider the structure of a military cartridge. In a unitary cartridge, the bullet, that is, the projectile, the powder charge and the primer are placed in one cartridge case. The primer sits in the base of the case. When struck by the hammer, it ignites the powder in the cartridge. The primer composition contains an initiating substance, lead styphnate, a fuel, antimony, and an oxidiser, potassium chlorate. The firing chain is as follows: the hammer strikes the primer, the primer composition ignites, the powder burns, the pressure of the powder gases rises, and the bullet moves along the barrel.

t: Special bullets and types of powder
n: We consider special bullets and types of powder. The armour-piercing bullet has a core of special steel. The incendiary bullet contains phosphorus, and the tracer bullet compounds of barium and magnesium. The explosive bullet breaks into small pieces on hitting the target; international agreements prohibit it in combat. Attention: smokeless powder is made from nitrocellulose and is used in military and sporting weapons, while black powder is used mainly in hunting and signal weapons. When 1 g of black powder burns, about 300 cubic cm of gas is formed. With smokeless powder there is three times as much, so the bullet carries further.

We consider the shot cartridge and hunting cartridges. The case of a shot cartridge is made of brass, plastic or cardboard; black powder may be used as the charge. The powder is closed with a felt, cardboard or plastic wad, the shot is poured on top, and it too is closed with a wad. Shot means small pellets with a diameter from 1 mm to 5.5 mm; anything larger is called buckshot. The slug cartridge of a smooth-bore hunting weapon contains a spherical lead bullet more than 10 mm in diameter, a Jakan or Brenneke slug.

t: Case analysis 1: features of the weapon and cartridge
n: Case analysis: features of the weapon and cartridge. A rifle with a shortened barrel and stock was brought for examination. Is it a typical or an atypical weapon? A weapon that is home-made or modified for some purpose is called atypical, while one made in special production is typical. The barrel of military and sporting weapons has 4-6 helical grooves, which impart to the bullet rotation about its axis. Question: what cartridge is used in a smooth-bore hunting weapon? What is the difference between shot and buckshot?

We consider the injuring factors of a shot. Powder burns in 0.01-0.001 s and produces gas pressure; in a rifled barrel the pressure is 2000-3000 atm. The gas pressure pushes the weapon slightly backwards. The barrel of a home-made weapon may burst and injure the person holding it. Groups of factors: the main projectile, that is, the bullet, shot and their parts; additional factors, namely the air ahead of the bullet, flame, gas, soot and powder; the weapon and its parts; and the secondary projectile, that is, clothing, a fragment of bone or an obstacle. Attention: the main and secondary projectiles are not the same.

t: Types of mechanical action: rupturing, tearing-out, wedge-like
n: We consider the types of mechanical action: rupturing, tearing-out and wedge-like. In rupturing action the energy is several thousand joules, and the wound is several times larger than the projectile. In tearing-out action the energy is several hundred joules, the tissue defect is smaller, and the edges are smooth. In wedge-like action the energy is several tens of joules, and the wound is slit-like or stellate, without a defect. In tearing-out action a tissue defect, that is, minus-tissue, is formed; N.I. Pirogov described it in 1849 and called this state loss of independence of the tissue. In wedge-like action there is no tissue defect; the exit hole is usually formed by this action.

t: Mechanical, thermal and chemical action of the additional factors
n: We consider the action of the additional factors. In mechanical action, the air ahead of the bullet at 3-5 cm gives a tissue defect, an abrasion collar and a flap-like tear; powder gases at 10-15 cm form abrasion, bruising and tearing. Soot, powder and metal particles give only a superficial, slight contusion effect, that is, a bruising effect, on the skin. In thermal action, the muzzle flame at 3-10 cm may burn clothing, skin and hair; the flame arises from the explosion of unburnt powder particles. The chemical action is due to the powder gases: carboxyhaemoglobin forms in the blood and carboxymyoglobin in the muscles, and the area around the entrance hole takes on a pink tint.

Quick questions: injuring factors. First question: what action is it if the energy is several thousand joules? Answer: rupturing. The wound is several times larger than the bullet, with uneven edges and radial tears. Second question: and several hundred joules? Answer: tearing-out. A tissue defect forms, the edges are smooth, and the size is smaller than the bullet diameter. Third question: and several tens of joules? Answer: wedge-like. There is no tissue defect, and the wound is slit-like or stellate; the exit hole most often forms this way. Attention: tearing-out and wedge-like actions are not the same; in tearing-out there is a defect, and in wedge-like there is not. The air ahead of the bullet acts at 3-5 cm, and powder gases at 10-15 cm.

We distinguish the range and distance of firing. The range is a set of features, while the distance is the length between the muzzle and the target. They are not the same thing. The range may be contact, close or not close, and it is determined by characteristic features on the clothing and body. When firing different weapons, the same range may correspond to a different distance. The distance is found by experiment: shots are fired from that same weapon and cartridge at a similar object from various distances.

We consider injury in contact firing. Three kinds of contact shot are distinguished: fully hermetic, full, and angled. In a fully hermetic shot, an imprint of the muzzle remains. In a full contact shot, the muzzle is wholly in contact; powder gases may rupture the internal organs, the wound edges are everted, and there are tears. In an angled contact shot, the particles lie in a tongue-like pattern and the tear is at one angle. At the beginning of the wound channel the soft tissue is pink, because carboxyhaemoglobin and carboxymyoglobin are formed.

We consider the three zones of close range. By the signs of action of the additional factors, three zones are distinguished at close range. In the first zone there are powder gas, soot, particles and oil; the distance is about 1 cm for the Makarov, 3 for the AK, and about 5 cm for a rifle. In the second zone there is no gas trace, but there are soot, powder and metal; 25-35 cm for many weapons. In the third zone only powder and metal particles; 150 cm for the Makarov, 200 for the AK, and 250 cm for a rifle. As the distance between the barrel and the target increases, the surface area covered by soot and particles grows. Attention: in smooth-bore hunting guns the third zone may reach 500 cm.

t: Close range: when there is an obstacle
n: We consider the case of an obstacle at close range. If there is an obstacle between the muzzle and the victim, the bullet pierces it and hits the target. In this case all the additional factors remain on the obstacle. On interacting with the obstacle, the bullet may be deformed and partly or completely broken up; its energy decreases and its direction changes. As a result, atypical injuries are inflicted, unlike those usually produced by that weapon, at that range and distance.

t: Non-close range and the Vinogradov phenomenon
n: Non-close range and the Vinogradov phenomenon. At non-close range, signs of the action of the additional factors around the entrance hole are not detected. For the Vinogradov phenomenon, the bullet velocity must be at least 500 m/s, the clothing must not be adhering to the body, and there must be no strong wind. At close range the outer layer of clothing bears soot; there is a lot of it, and it decreases from the centre to the edge. In the Vinogradov phenomenon there is no soot on the outer layer; the soot is on the inner layer and the body, around the hole, much less of it, and it increases towards the periphery. Attention: the Vinogradov phenomenon is not close range.

Case analysis: determining the range. On a corpse, only powder and metal particles were found around the entrance hole, with no signs of the action of powder gases. Question: which zone does this correspond to? These signs are characteristic of the third zone of close range: up to 150 cm for the Makarov pistol. To determine the exact distance, using that same weapon and cartridge, experimental shots are fired at similar targets and the results are compared. Attention: the range is a set of features, while the distance is the length between the muzzle and the target. They are not the same thing.

t: Mechanism of injury: the impact-action theory
n: We consider the mechanism of injury: the impact-action theory. The injury depends on three groups of factors: the properties of the projectile, ballistics, and the properties of the injured region. A strong blow falls on a small area, spreads sideways as a compression wave, and phases of positive and negative pressure alternate. The force of the blow spreads sideways and backwards as well; the temporary cavities formed pulsate. In the wound wall there are three zones: the channel, the zone of contusion (from 0.3 to 1-2 cm) and the zone of concussion (4-5 cm or more).

t: Types of wound and the wound channel
n: We consider the types of wound and the wound channel. In a perforating injury three parts are distinguished: the entrance hole, the wound channel and the exit hole. In a blind wound there is no exit hole, and the projectile remains at the end of the channel. In a tangential injury the bullet does not enter fully: an elongated abrasion or a furrow-like wound is formed. The wound channel may be straight, broken or arc-shaped. An interrupted channel arises from contraction of tissues and usually indicates that the injury was vital. A bullet with a displaced centre of gravity loses stability in the body; the energy is given up to the tissue more fully, resulting in a large channel, rupture of internal organs and bone fractures.

We distinguish the entrance and exit holes. The entrance hole is round or oval, a tissue defect is often present, the edges are smooth and turned inwards, and there are an abrasion collar and a contamination collar. The exit hole is slit-like, arc-shaped or stellate, a defect is rarely present, the edges are uneven and turned outwards, and collars are usually absent. At the entrance hole there is a sleeve-like haemorrhage and the tissues are separated into layers. At the exit the haemorrhages are asymmetric and the tissues are not separated into layers. Attention: in thin regions, that is, the forearm and upper arm, a defect may also be present at the exit, with the tip pointing outwards.

We consider the collars and changes in bones. At the edge of the entrance, an abrasion collar 1-3 mm wide is formed, and its outer diameter equals the diameter of the bullet; in soft regions, that is, the abdomen and buttocks, it is wider. Soot and oil on the bullet's surface form a contamination collar at the skin edge. The two collars lie one on top of the other; this is described in Pirogov's book (1865). In a flat bone, a defect in the shape of a truncated cone forms at the point of bullet entry, and the direction of the projectile is from the smaller base to the larger base. In a long bone, at the entrance there is a round defect with radial cracks; at the exit the defect is larger and the cracks run lengthwise.

t: Quick question 3: entrance and exit hole
n: Quick questions: entrance and exit hole. First question: which hole is round or oval, with relatively smooth edges turned inwards? Answer: the entrance hole. Second question: where is the abrasion and contamination collar found? Answer: at the entrance hole; at the exit hole it is most often absent. Third question: which hole is characterised by a tissue defect? Answer: the entrance hole; at the exit it is rarely found. Attention, there is a risk of error: the exit hole is larger, slit-like or stellate, with edges turned outwards. Do not confuse it with the entrance hole.

t: Injuries from shot and blank cartridges
n: We consider injuries from shot and blank cartridges. A shot cartridge is used in a smooth-bore hunting gun; blind wounds are usually formed. In a contact shot or at a distance up to 1 m, the action is compact, and a single hole equals the diameter of the cartridge. Up to 5 m there is relative scatter: a main hole and small wounds around it. Beyond 5 m there is scatter, and small, similar wounds appear. A blank cartridge has no bullet: in a contact shot or from close range the injury is inflicted by the powder gases, and a large defect and torn edges form. In a contact shot a blind wound and rupture of internal organs are possible; at a few cm there is no serious injury.

t: Injuries from gas and pneumatic weapons
n: We consider injuries from gas and pneumatic weapons. A gas weapon temporarily incapacitates with an irritant, that is, a substance irritating the eyes, nose, throat and airways. The action appears at 2-3 m and lasts about an hour. Signs: pain, cough, lacrimation, blepharospasm. Complications: keratitis, conjunctivitis, bronchitis, pneumonia; residual effects are determined for up to 7 days. In forensic chemical examination, traces of the irritant are taken from skin, clothing and objects with a gauze swab moistened with ethyl alcohol and sent to the laboratory in a sealed container. The bullet of a pneumatic weapon flies by compressed air and reaches 30-50 m; there are no traces of additional factors, the wound is blind, and sometimes a severe injury leads to death.

t: Questions of examination in fatal cases
n: We consider the questions of examination in fatal cases. First of all it is established whether the injury was inflicted by a firearm, and from what weapon and with what projectile. The range, distance, entrance and exit holes and the direction of the wound channel are examined. Questions are also asked about the relative position of the barrel and the victim, the sequence of injuries, whether the weapon was automatic, and whether the injury was inflicted by the victim himself. In the sequence, the haemorrhage is more pronounced in the first injury, soot and metal particles are more abundant in the later one, and oil particles are more abundant in the first. With an automatic weapon, firing up to 900 rounds per minute, there are many close injuries on one side; the shape of the hole, the direction of the channel and the range are not distinguishable.

t: Methods of examination and medical documents
n: We consider the methods of examination and medical documents. In examination of the corpse, instrumental and laboratory methods are added to macroscopic and microscopic examination. X-rays and Bucky rays reveal the bullet, shot and metal around the hole. Contact-diffusion and spectral methods show the presence and type of metal. Ultraviolet light reveals a small amount of soot and oil, and infrared photography reveals soot, powder and metal on dark clothing. During treatment the signs of the injury change, so the physician must record the holes and the channel fully in the medical document. The bullet in the wound channel, shot, clothing and footwear are handed over in packaging to the law enforcement bodies.

t: Case analysis 3: the question of self-infliction
n: Case analysis: the question of self-infliction. Suppose a firearm is found beside the corpse. There are traces of soot on the surfaces of the hands and in the nostrils and ears. Traces of the victim's blood were found at the tip of the barrel and on the palm; this may suggest that he fired it himself. It is checked whether he could have pulled the trigger himself, and whether the range and distance of firing and the direction of the wound channel correspond. Question: why can no conclusion be drawn from a single feature? The question is resolved by establishing a number of circumstances together.

We consider blast trauma: concept and types. An explosion is the release of a large amount of energy in a very short time as a result of a physical or chemical change of substances. It is divided into three kinds: natural, that is, lightning, a volcano, a meteorite; intentional, that is, explosives; and accidental, that is, gas cylinders and steam boilers. An explosive substance is transformed by combustion or detonation. Combustion is slower, but in a closed environment it accelerates: black powder burns at up to 400 m/s. Detonation occurs under the action of a shock wave, and its speed is several thousand m/s; in TNT the pressure exceeds one hundred thousand atmospheres. Attention: combustion and detonation are not the same.

We study the classification of explosives. By state of aggregation, explosives are solid, liquid and gaseous. Primary, that is, initiating, substances are very sensitive, so they are part of the primers of firearms and of detonators; for example mercury fulminate. Secondary, that is, high-explosive, substances are set off by the action of detonation, for example TNT and ammonal; they are used in shells, grenades, mines, bombs, construction and mining. Propellants burn with decomposition, for example gunpowder. A pyrotechnic composition consists of a mixture of an oxidiser and a fuel.

t: Explosion: types of action (according to Popov)
n: We consider the types of action of an explosion according to V.L. Popov. The factors of an explosion cause mechanical, thermal, chemical and baroacoustic damage. Mechanical action includes gas, particles, the shock wave, fragments of the device and projectiles; the mechanical action of the explosion gases gives rupture, contused wound and bruising in the skin and under it. In thermal action the skin and hair are burnt, and clothing and objects burn. In chemical action carboxyhaemoglobin is formed; particles of the explosive act mainly superficially, in a complex manner. Baroacoustic trauma arises mainly from the shock wave of the surroundings: damage to the tympanic membrane and lungs is possible.

t: Injuring factors and action of an explosion
n: We look once more at the injuring factors and action of an explosion. The types of action: mechanical, thermal, chemical and baroacoustic. In baroacoustic trauma, damage to the tympanic membrane and lungs is possible. There are five factors: detonation products, the shock wave of the surroundings, fragments of the device, special means and secondary projectiles. The shock wave strikes like an unbounded flat blunt body. The speed of fragments of the device reaches several thousand m/s. Special means, that is, nails, bolts, fuel, and toxic and biological substances, cause various injuries and infection.

We distinguish the action of the shock wave, fragments and projectiles. The shock wave acts like an unbounded flat blunt body: on the side of the centre of the explosion a mechanical injury forms, and on the opposite surface an injury from impact. The initial speed of fragments of the device is up to several thousand m/s; they produce abrasions, bruises, wounds, bone fractures and sometimes separation of body parts. Secondary projectiles inflict mainly mechanical injuries, milder than those from fragments; secondary ignition causes thermal injury. Burning of synthetic materials and coatings may lead, besides thermal injury, to poisoning by toxic substances.

We consider the distances of an explosion. Four conventional distances of an explosion are distinguished: contact, close, relatively close and not close. At contact distance, detonation products and fragments act. At close distance, gases, fragments and the shock wave. At relatively close distance, the shock wave, fragments and secondary projectiles. At non-close distance, fragments and secondary projectiles. The exact distance of each depends on the explosive, the properties of the device and the power of the charge. Attention: at close distance detonation products are present, and at relatively close distance secondary projectiles are added.

Case analysis: an explosion incident. When a device without a charge explodes, the nature of the injury depends on the type of device, the intervening distance and the surrounding objects. When gas cylinders explode, the main injuries are inflicted by fragments of the cylinder wall. When a steam boiler explodes, injuries are mainly thermal. When natural gas, coal dust and flour dust explode, mechanical injury from the shock wave is added. Question: in which explosion is the leading injury from fragments, and in which from thermal action? Why?

t: Explosion examination and the physician's tasks
n: We consider the examination of an explosion and the physician's tasks. In examination of an explosion, besides the type and nature of the injury, the properties of the explosive and the device and the distance of the explosion are determined. In the explosion of a device without a charge, the injury depends on the type of device, the intervening distance and the surrounding objects. In a gas cylinder the injury is mainly from fragments of the cylinder wall; in a steam boiler it is thermal; with gas, coal and flour dust it is thermal and mechanical from the shock wave. The physician fully examines and documents the injuries of the body, and within a short time hands over to the law enforcement bodies foreign bodies on the clothing and body.

Let us sum up. The range is a set of features: contact, close, non-close. The distance is the length between the muzzle and the target. Remember: range and distance are not the same. The questions resolved by examination: whether a shot was fired from a weapon, the entrance and exit holes, the direction of the channel, the sequence of injuries and self-infliction. The physician must record the injuries fully and quickly hand over any foreign bodies found to the law enforcement bodies. Review questions: how a firearm injury differs from other mechanical injury; the structure of a cartridge; the difference between range and distance.
